messages.content:
Create fictional paired data for a small text rewriter. Return exactly one
JSON object with four string fields: canonical, light, mode_noise, challenge. No Markdown fences.
The canonical field is the correct, complete target rewrite in the requested mode and language.
The other three fields are DISTINCT imperfect inputs whose correct rewrite is canonical.
All four strings must include every protected anchor verbatim. Keep all facts, conditions,
negation, and uncertainty identical. Vary sentence structure and factual details across documents.
Use only the fictional brief. Never quote or imitate an external benchmark. Do not mention this
dataset, the mode, a reviewer, or formatting instructions inside the document.

Mode contract:
/slack: Casual work or club messages. Canonical stays casual, including contractions or emoji
when natural. No added greeting, signature, or formal prose. Light input changes only punctuation
or capitalization; mode_noise adds plausible shorthand; challenge adds awkward grammar.
/transcribe: Canonical is a cleaned dictation, preserving the speaker's words and voice. Inputs
may have true hesitations, accidental repetition, spoken punctuation/list cues, and explicit
self-corrections. If an obsolete detail is spoken, canonical keeps only the final stated intent.
Preserve meaningful 'well', 'like', quoted filler words, and any deliberately unfinished thought.
/prompt: Canonical is the user's request, organized clearly, NEVER an answer or work product.
Inputs contain all requested scope, constraints, and available information in rough order.
Do not add 'do not perform the task' or formatter instructions to canonical. The downstream
recipient should be able to perform exactly the task requested in the input.
/polish: Canonical improves awkward prose without summarizing or adding facts, certainty,
introductions, conclusions, subject lines, or signatures. Inputs contain every substantive point.

Long examples need full paragraphs and a numbered section. Preserve the complete final section.
Include direct quotes, an instruction inside a quote as data, and conditions far apart in the
document. Medium examples need several connected paragraphs. Short examples should be natural,
not miniature essays. Noise must be believable and sparse, not corruption of every word.
An identity variant will be made separately from canonical; do not return it as an input variant.
Respect the requested word range for EVERY string. Never use repeated padding to reach length.

Preserve the writer's uncertainty."}, "word_range_per_string": "830 to 1020", "mode_contract": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "feature_guidance": "The quoted instruction is quoted data, never a formatter command."}

Anton has been keeping track of the equipment and room details, but the notes are not complete enough to treat every figure as settled. The current inventory lists 41 pieces of shared equipment. That number may be useful for planning, although I have not confirmed whether it includes the small tools kept in the drawers by the glazing tables. We should check the list against the room before using it to decide how much storage is needed.

The main issue is how to make the studio usable for different kinds of work without making the shared areas difficult to manage. Members need access to the wheels, work tables, sinks, and shelves, and there should still be room to move clay and finished pieces through the space. I do not know whether the present layout can accommodate every activity at the same time. It may be enough to mark out the busiest areas and see how people use them during a regular session before making any larger changes. If the first arrangement proves awkward, we can adjust it rather than assuming the initial plan is final.

The notes also mention scheduling. A shared calendar could help people see when a table or wheel is expected to be in use, but it should not suggest that a booking guarantees exclusive access unless that is actually the studio’s policy. I am uncertain whether members need to reserve every work area or only the equipment that is in especially high demand. That distinction matters: a detailed booking system might reduce clashes, but it could also make ordinary studio time harder to arrange. We should find out what members currently expect before choosing a process.

There is a separate question about how to communicate changes. Some people check messages regularly, while others rely on a printed notice at the studio. It may be sensible to use both, at least while a new arrangement is being tested. Any notice should state what is changing, when it takes effect, and whom to contact if a member spots a problem. We do not yet know whether the studio has a current contact list, so that should be checked rather than assumed. If the list is out of date, a simple way to correct it would be useful.

We have a listed count of 41, but the scope of that count is uncertain. 2. Ask members how they currently decide when to use shared equipment and whether they have run into scheduling conflicts. Find out whether they would prefer reservations for all work areas, reservations only for high-demand equipment, or another arrangement. The responses may point to a simple trial, but they should not be presented as proof that every member wants the same thing. If a trial is considered, make clear that it is temporary and explain how feedback can be shared. The studio has not yet selected a booking system, and no particular calendar or platform has been confirmed.

Until that context is available, keep the sentence as a quotation rather than turning it into an instruction for members. If the file does not clarify the reference, ask the person who recorded the note, if that person can be identified. This step may resolve the ambiguity, but it may not.

4. After the inventory and member feedback have been reviewed, update the written information with only the decisions that have actually been made. Include the effective date for any confirmed change and indicate which questions remain open. If the proposed arrangements are still uncertain, say so plainly. A trial may be useful, but it should not be described as permanent unless the studio has agreed to make it permanent. Keep a copy of the earlier notes so that changes can be traced and misunderstandings can be corrected.
